Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Expectation2: Provide initial medical care to patients
Situation2: The ambulance driver is conducting a routine check of the first-aid kit to ensure all supplies are present and not expired.
Story: I was halfway through checking the first-aid kit in the back of the ambulance, making sure every bandage and vial was accounted for, when my phone buzzed. It was Sam, my closest friend. His voice trembled as he asked if I had a minute—he’d just had a huge fight with his partner and needed someone to talk to. I could hear the pain in his words, and I knew he expected me to listen, to be there for him like I always had. But the checklist in my hand reminded me of my duty; if I missed something, it could mean the difference between life and death for a patient later. My mind raced, torn between the urge to comfort Sam and the responsibility to ensure the ambulance was ready for the next emergency. I felt the weight of both roles pressing down on me, each demanding my full attention, and I stood there, phone in hand, heart pounding, caught between being the friend Sam needed and the ambulance driver my patients depended on.
